author: reek
body: The inspector pane TrackerApp, WorkflowHtml, CallPage and ItemDesignerApp all describe themselves as using. None of them renders one: `call-participant-detail`, `item-detail` and `wf-process-detail` are each mentioned exactly twice, at their signature and their definition, and neither `detail-widget` nor `detail-overlay` has a caller in `apps/`. Latent, and therefore unmeasured.

author: reek
body: The pane assembles itself out of four optional sections, so the shape it produces depends on which of them are present. Asking with all of them filled cannot tell a section that is conditional from one that is always emitted, so the empty spec is asked first and each section is added in turn.

author: reek
body: The badge is the field kind worth the most attention. `df-badge` takes a colour and all four real callers compute one to pass: CallPage derives one from mute, video and screen-share state, ItemDesignerApp calls `badge-label-color`, TrackerApp calls `tk-status-color`, WorkflowHtml calls `wf-status-badge-color`. Each now passes a TONE beside it and the render arm applies it.

author: reek
body: **The priority bar carries its COUNT now**, so Urgent and None no longer come out identical. `badge-widget` renders a gauge of bars against four rather than a fixed 12x12 custom node, which is the shape that already carries a quantity and that every renderer in the tree draws.

author: reek
body: This test asked that question before the fix and read `same=yes`, which is what it was built to pin. It went on reading `same=yes` for a moment after the fix too, because `payload` answered the bare word "gauge" for the one kind that carries numbers while every other arm printed its contents. A helper named for the payload has to print the payload; the category is never the assertion.

author: reek
body: A pane with nothing but a title is a header and a separator. Each optional section adds its own separator and heading, so the child count is what says whether a section was emitted at all.

author: reek
body: Subtitle, then title, then a close button. The order is printed rather than judged: an identifier ahead of a name is a real convention and this records what the pane does rather than what a reader expects.

author: reek
body: Each field is a row of a fixed-width label and a flexed value. What the value widget IS differs by kind, and that is the assertion.

author: reek
body: A badge and a text field are built from the same string here, so the only difference that can appear is the one being a badge is supposed to make. The size is printed as well as the payload, because the payload alone cannot see a size and a line blind to it would read as though the two were identical for a reason it had checked.

author: reek
body: **This line used to pin a defect and now pins a behaviour.** A plain `df-badge` still comes out identical to a text field, and that is correct: it names no tone, so it asks for none. What changed is that there is somewhere to put the meaning at all. `df-badge-toned` carries a tone, the render arm applies it, and the line below reads it back off the node.

author: reek
body: The pair is the point. The untoned badge staying identical to the text field is what stops the toned line passing for a reason it has not checked.

author: reek
body: The same question one chapter over, because DetailPane is not where a badge is supposed to be drawn. Every BadgeStyle carries a colour and BsPriorityBar carries a bar count as well.

author: reek
body: The colours themselves are computed correctly and differ, which is what makes the rendering the loss rather than the source.

target: section:What a caller still holding the spec sees
author: reek
body: `detail-add-field` pushes onto the spec's own list and hands back the same record. The original is read AFTER the call, not snapshotted before.
